content: Policies and guidelines on WikiDoc are established through a consensus process that involves revising multiple sources to ensure consistency and maintain high-quality standards. There is an ongoing debate between those who believe that rules should be explicitly stated and those who argue that written rules cannot account for every possible variation of problematic editing or behavior. Regardless of this debate, users who act against the spirit of the written policies may face reprimand, even if no specific rule has been technically violated. Editors who contribute in good faith, maintain civility, seek consensus, and work towards the goal of creating an excellent living textbook will find a welcoming environment. Definitions: Policies: Policies are widely accepted by editors and serve as standards that all users are expected to follow. Editors must ensure that any changes made to policy pages reflect consensus. The principle of a neutral point of view is fundamental and non-negotiable. Other core content policies include verifiability and the prohibition of original research. Together, these policies define the type and quality of material acceptable in WikiDoc articles. These policies are complementary and should not be interpreted in isolation. Editors are encouraged to familiarize themselves with all three. The principles underlying these policies are non-negotiable and cannot be overridden by other policies, guidelines, or editor consensus. Policy pages may only be edited to improve the application and explanation of these principles. Guidelines: Guidelines are advisory in nature and should be applied with common sense, allowing for occasional exceptions. Amendments to guidelines should be discussed on their respective talk pages, though minor edits to improve them are generally acceptable. Disputes over guideline wording are resolved through discussion, compromise, and consensus. Such disputes do not suspend the guideline or change its status. Voting on guidelines is discouraged, as it polarizes issues. Copyright and Copyleft: The manual of style and naming conventions are specific types of guidelines that address proper naming and article formatting. Guidelines are categorized for convenience, but there is no practical difference between the various types. They codify general practices that have already achieved wide consensus. Policies may evolve from well-used processes or proposals discussed on wiki pages. Changing policy often requires first changing common practice. Essays: Essays reflect the views of individual editors or groups of editors. They are not policies or guidelines, even if they represent a consensus. Essays can be written without formal proposals, but they do not necessarily represent the entire community. If an essay does not reflect general consensus, it may still convey the opinions of a significant group of editors. Ignoring or unilaterally changing such essays may lead to conflicts with those editors. Essays may sometimes be mislabeled due to the evolving nature of Wikipedia policies and guidelines. Proposals: Proposals are suggested guidelines, policies, or processes for which consensus has not yet been established. Amendments to proposals should be discussed on their talk pages. Proposals should be advertised to solicit feedback and achieve consensus. The status of a proposal is not determined by vote counts, as polling is not a substitute for discussion or consensus. Historical Pages: Historical pages document processes no longer in use or logs of past processes. These pages can be revived through proper advertisement. Rejected Pages: Rejected pages are proposals that fail to achieve consensus after a reasonable period of discussion or where consensus remains unclear. Rewriting a rejected proposal from scratch is often more effective than making minor changes. Feature Requests: Feature requests involve changes to the Wikipedia software. These should be discussed with developers before seeking community opinion to avoid moot discussions. Enforcement of Policies: WikiDoc editors enforce most policies and guidelines through editing and discussion. Administrators handle enforcement of certain policies, such as vandalism, by blocking users. In extreme cases, the Arbitration Committee addresses highly disruptive situations. Certain software features, like page deletion or locking, are restricted to administrators, who are trusted members of the community. Sources of WikiDoc Policies: WikiDoc policies are derived from various sources, including Wikipedia’s established policies and guidelines, as well as declarations related to copyright, legal issues, or server load. Commitment to Excellence Policy: As a WikiDoc editor, I acknowledge the following commitments: 1. I understand that the quality of my contributions reflects my personal commitment to excellence and Dr. Gibson’s commitment to quality. If I fail to uphold these standards, I may be asked to stop contributing. 2. I agree not to violate copyright laws or commit plagiarism. Violations may result in my resignation. 3. I commit to excellence by ensuring my content is well-written, grammatically correct, and properly formatted. I will conduct thorough research and cite sources appropriately. 4. I will respect team members and understand that disrespect may lead to my removal from the team. My letter of recommendation will reflect my teamwork and respect for others. WikiDoc may choose not to renew my appointment or rotate responsibilities as needed. WikiDoc Guidelines and Projects: WikiDoc projects often include subpages that explain project-specific practices or recommendations. These documents may represent the consensus of a small group of editors and are not classified as policies or guidelines unless sufficient consensus is reached. How-to or help pages provide instructions for specific actions and differ from guidelines, which explain when or why certain actions are recommended. Other Essays and Discussions: The Meta-Wiki site contains editorial-style articles about Wikipedia and related topics. Centralized discussions and templates are available for ongoing policy discussions and proposals. Internal and External Resources: Internal resources include governance documents, licensing information, and guidelines on avoiding plagiarism. External resources include lists of Wikipedia policies, guidelines, and discussions on new ideas and proposals.
